title: D. B. Cooper — the hijacker who jumped into the night and vanished
sources: Wikipedia: D. B. Cooper — on 24 November 1971 (Thanksgiving Eve) a man paid cash at Portland for a one-way ticket on Northwest Orient Flight 305 to Seattle, a 30-minute trip, under the name 'Dan Cooper'; he wore a dark suit, white shirt, thin black tie and raincoat, sat in 18-E and ordered a bourbon and 7-Up; he handed a note to flight attendant Florence Schaffner, who put it unopened in her purse assuming it was a phone number; he leaned over: 'Miss, you'd better look at that note. I have a bomb.'; his briefcase showed a battery wired to red cylinders; he demanded $200,000 and four parachutes; the plane circled for about two hours; at Seattle he released the 36 passengers in exchange for the money (10,000 unmarked $20 bills) and the parachutes; he ordered a flight to Mexico City at minimum speed, below 10,000 ft, with the aft door open and the airstair down; two F-106 fighters followed out of sight; around 8 pm a warning light showed the airstair had been deployed; the plane landed in Reno at 11:02 pm with the stairs still down and Cooper gone; he had parachuted over the forests of southwest Washington; a reporter's error made him 'D. B. Cooper'; agents recovered his clip-on tie; on 10 February 1980, eight-year-old Brian Ingram, raking sand for a campfire on the Columbia River bank, found three packets of the ransom money (about $5,800); the FBI suspended its investigation in 2016; it remains the only unsolved air piracy in commercial aviation history

Photos (public domain, Wikimedia Commons / FBI / US Air Force): the FBI composite sketches; the original Flight 305 ticket; a Northwest Orient Boeing 727, 1970; a Boeing 727-100; the ransom money found in 1980; the 'Cooper vane' later fitted to 727s so the rear stairs could not be lowered in flight

Archive film (public domain): 'The Columbia' (Bonneville Power Administration, 1949) — the Columbia River and its gorge; 'USAF William Tell Gunnery Exhibition 1965' (US Air Force) — F-106 Delta Dart fighters — illustrative
Music: Beethoven, Moonlight Sonata (1st mvt) — Paul Pitman for Musopen, public domain

post.facebook:
In 1971, a man hijacked a plane, took $200,000, and jumped out into the night. Nobody ever found him.

The day before Thanksgiving, he paid cash for a one-way ticket from Portland to Seattle under the name "Dan Cooper". Dark suit, black tie, raincoat. He ordered a bourbon and handed a stewardess a note — she thought it was his phone number and dropped it in her purse. He leaned over: "Miss, you'd better look at that note. I have a bomb."

His briefcase was full of wires and red cylinders. He wanted $200,000 and four parachutes. In Seattle he swapped the passengers for the money, then ordered the plane back into the air towards Mexico — slow, low, with the rear stairs open, two fighter jets following out of sight. At about 8 p.m. a warning light came on: the stairs were down. When the plane landed in Reno, he was gone.

The FBI searched for years and found nothing. Then in 1980 an eight-year-old boy building a campfire on the Columbia River found rotting bundles of $20 bills — the serial numbers matched. The rest of the money, and the man, have never been found.

It is still the only unsolved hijacking in the history of commercial aviation. Who was D. B. Cooper? 👇

youtube.description:
In 1971, a man hijacked a plane, took $200,000, and jumped out into the night. Nobody ever found him.

"Dan Cooper" boarded Northwest Orient Flight 305 in Portland, told a flight attendant he had a bomb, swapped the passengers for $200,000 and four parachutes in Seattle, and parachuted from the rear stairs over the forests of southwest Washington. In 1980 an eight-year-old found some of the ransom on the Columbia River. The rest — and the man — were never found. It remains the only unsolved hijacking in commercial aviation history.
